cards.front: Can a static method be overridden?
cards.back: No — static methods are resolved at compile time, and overriding is a runtime concern
cards.extra: A subclass can declare a method with the same signature, but it hides rather than overrides. Called through the superclass type, the parent's version runs.
cards.source: baeldung.com — A Guide to the Static Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::04 Static Keyword
cards.example:
class Base { static String f() { return "Base"; } }
class Sub extends Base { // @Override static String f() -> error: static methods cannot be annotated with @Override
  static String f() { return "Sub"; } }
class Ex { static void demo() { Base b = new Sub(); System.out.println(b.f()); } }

cards.front: Can an instance method access static members directly?
cards.back: Yes — an instance method can use both instance and static members
cards.extra: The reverse is not true: a static method has no object, so instance members are out of reach without a reference.
cards.source: baeldung.com — A Guide to the Static Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::04 Static Keyword
cards.example:
class Ex { static int count; int id;
  void instanceMethod() { count++; System.out.println(id + ":" + count); }
  static void demo() { new Ex().instanceMethod(); } }

cards.front: What are the two legitimate reasons for a static block?
cards.back: Multi-statement initialisation, and initialisation that needs its own exception handling
cards.extra: A field initialiser is a single expression. If you need a loop, a try/catch or several dependent assignments, the block is the tool.
cards.source: baeldung.com — A Guide to the Static Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::04 Static Keyword
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static int config;
  static { int a = 1, b = 2; config = a + b; } // multi-statement init
  static { try { config = Integer.parseInt("3"); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { config = 0; } }
}

cards.front: What is the difference in member access between an inner class and a static nested class?
cards.back: An inner class sees all members of the outer class, including private ones; a static nested class sees only the outer's static members
cards.extra: The static variant has no enclosing instance, so instance state can only be reached through an explicit reference.
cards.source: baeldung.com — A Guide to the Static Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
class Ex { private int p = 1; private static int s = 2;
  class Inner { int read() { return p + s; } }
  static class Nested { int read() { return s; } } // p needs an explicit Ex reference
}

cards.front: What is the initialization-on-demand holder singleton?
cards.back: A private static nested class holding public static final Singleton INSTANCE, returned from a static accessor
cards.extra: The nested class is loaded only when the accessor is first called, so the instance is created lazily — and class initialisation is already thread-safe, so no synchronization is needed.
cards.source: baeldung.com — A Guide to the Static Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects
cards.example:
class Singleton {
  private Singleton() {}
  private static class Holder { public static final Singleton INSTANCE = new Singleton(); }
  public static Singleton getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }
}

cards.front: Why prefer a static nested class when it needs no outer instance?
cards.back: It avoids coupling to the outer instance and needs no enclosing-object memory
cards.extra: A non-static inner class carries a hidden reference to its outer object, which is pure overhead if it is never used.
cards.source: baeldung.com — A Guide to the Static Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
class Ex { static class Helper { int twice(int n) { return 2 * n; } }
  static void demo() { System.out.println(new Helper().twice(3)); } } // no enclosing Ex instance

cards.front: What causes "non-static variable cannot be referenced from a static context"?
cards.back: Using an instance field or method inside a static method, where no object exists
cards.extra: The compiler cannot know which object you mean. Fix it by passing an instance in, or by making the member static.
cards.source: baeldung.com — A Guide to the Static Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::04 Static Keyword
cards.example:
class Ex {
  int instance = 1; static void m() {
    // System.out.println(instance); // error: no object exists here
    System.out.println(new Ex().instance); // works through an object
  }
}

cards.front: What does a static nested class have in common with a top-level class?
cards.back: It behaves the same way — it is simply packaged inside the class that uses it
cards.extra: Same rules, same capabilities; the nesting is for encapsulation and readability, not for different semantics.
cards.source: baeldung.com — A Guide to the Static Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes
cards.example:
class Ex { static class Nested { int n = 1; }
  static void demo() { Nested x = new Nested(); System.out.println(x.n); } } // like a top-level class

cards.front: Since when do static fields exist, and until when?
cards.back: For as long as the class is loaded — not for the lifetime of any object
cards.extra: They are created at class initialisation and shared by every instance; they disappear only when the class is unloaded.
cards.source: baeldung.com — A Guide to the Static Keyword in Java
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::04 Static Keyword
cards.example:
class Ex { static int created; Ex() { created++; }
  static void demo() { Ex a = new Ex(); a = null;
    System.out.println(created); } }   // field outlives the object
